title: Saudi Arabia Cuts Asian Oil Prices to a Six-Year Low as Google Bets $4.3B on Nuclear
subhead: Aramco slashed its November Arab Light price for Asia to the widest discount since 2020, absorbing record freight costs to defend market share, while Google signed a 20-year deal to add 890 MW of nuclear capacity to the PJM grid.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Absorbs the Freight Bill to Hold Asia
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco cut its November official selling price for Arab Light crude to Asia by $3 a barrel, setting it at $5 below the Oman/Dubai average — the widest discount since June 2020, according to Reuters data cited by Tekedia. Heavier Arab Medium and Arab Heavy grades were cut by $5 a barrel.

The move blindsided the market: a Reuters survey had forecast an increase of as much as $5 a barrel, in line with rising Middle East benchmarks. The reason is cost, not demand. The daily rate to time-charter a VLCC carrying 2 million barrels from the Gulf to China hit $1.2 million on Friday, versus roughly $80,000 a day a year earlier, per LSEG data. Three Asian refining sources told Reuters the lower OSPs are designed to compensate buyers for those freight costs, longer voyages and delays at Egypt's Sidi Kerir terminal.

The signal is straightforward: Riyadh would rather eat margin than lose share in the world's biggest consuming region while war-driven shipping disruptions scramble the physical market.
sections.whyItMatters: Pricing power in crude is shifting from producer to logistics. The headline Brent price no longer reflects what Asian refiners actually pay — Saudi Arabia is now subsidizing the risk premium its customers carry.

sections.heading: Google and Constellation Lock In 890 MW of Nuclear for AI
sections.body:
Constellation Energy signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Google supporting 890 MW of new nuclear capacity in the PJM grid, backed by $4.3 billion in new Constellation investment, Utility Dive reported. The capacity comes through uprates of 11 existing units across Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, with the first uprate expected online in 2028. The two companies also signed a 15-year supply agreement for a further 2,700 MW across PJM.

It follows a 690-MW deal Constellation struck with Amazon the prior week, centered on a $3-billion, 190-MW expansion of the Calvert Cliffs plant in Maryland, due online between 2030 and 2032. Constellation said the Google deal is a direct response to PJM's 'Bring Your Own Power' proposal and the White House's ratepayer-protection pledge. PJM is short roughly 6.8 GW of new capacity as data-center demand rises and has delayed a reliability backstop auction after FERC only partly approved it on Sept. 29.

Nuclear equities rallied on the news: Constellation jumped about 12%, Vistra 8% and Talen 7%, per 247wallst.
sections.whyItMatters: Hyperscalers are becoming the de facto financiers of firm baseload power. The AI buildout is now a structural demand driver for nuclear expansion in the US — funded by private tech capital rather than ratepayers.

sections.heading: EIA Hikes Forecasts Again as Inventories Drain
sections.body:
The US Energy Information Administration raised its oil price forecast for both this year and next, citing rapidly falling global stockpiles and tight diesel markets caused by the Iran war. In its Short-Term Energy Outlook, the EIA now expects Brent to average about $98 a barrel in 2026 — up 8% from its prior forecast — and about $105 in Q4 2026, $14 above the previous estimate. US retail diesel, which hit record highs last month, is expected to stay above $6 a gallon in October before easing toward roughly $4.50 in 2027.

The EIA also flagged the workarounds keeping barrels moving: Saudi Arabia's restart of East-West Pipeline shipments to the Red Sea, plus 'dark transits' in which tankers disable tracking before transferring cargo at sea. Those measures restored Gulf flows excluding Iran to more than 81% of pre-war levels in September. The agency expects crude production shut-ins to fall from 4.5 million bpd in Q4 2026 to 2.7 million bpd in Q1 2027, and Brent to average $84 in 2027.
sections.whyItMatters: The official US forecaster now treats the disruption as a durable, multi-quarter supply event rather than a spike. The diesel number is the one to watch — it hits trucking, agriculture and heating, and it is not coming down quickly.

sections.heading: EU Prepares Its Largest Russia Sanctions Package Since 2022
sections.body:
EU ambassadors are expected to approve roughly 1,650 new designations against Russia on Wednesday — the bloc's largest package since the 2022 full-scale invasion, Reuters reported via UNN. About 1,570 entries target organizations and individuals tied to Russia's defense-industrial complex, with more than half focused on missile production. The measures impose EU travel bans, transaction bans and asset freezes. Lists go to EU foreign ministers next Monday for final approval.

The package is notably defense-heavy rather than energy-first, though it lands as separate reporting shows the sanctions-evasion network still moving fuel. A Guardian analysis of port and ship-tracking records found that South Korea shipped more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel — mostly diesel — to Russia in July and August aboard sanctioned tankers, as Ukrainian drone strikes disrupted Russian refining. Seoul, which backs Ukraine, has drawn criticism from Kyiv over the flows. Japan separately imposed its first sanctions on 35 Russian shadow-fleet tankers on October 2, per Army Recognition.
sections.whyItMatters: The evasion architecture is now a two-way street: refining capacity inside Russia is degraded, so Moscow imports product while it exports crude. Sanctions packages that target defense but leave the fuel loop open will keep financing the war.

sections.heading: Rare Earth Prices Spike Ahead of Pentagon Sourcing Deadline
sections.body:
Prices for the heavy rare earths dysprosium and terbium outside China surged sharply in the week to October 1, with buyers front-running US defense-sector restrictions that take effect in January 2027. According to Fastmarkets, terbium oxide rose 41% to $5,000–8,000 per kg, dysprosium oxide climbed to $2,500–3,500 per kg, and ferro-dysprosium jumped to $2,750–3,850 per kg from $1,375–2,100 a week earlier — one of the strongest weekly gains in the market.

The trigger is a coming Pentagon prohibition on procuring samarium-cobalt and neodymium-iron-boron magnets containing material mined, refined, separated, melted or produced in China, starting January 2027. Fastmarkets noted US buyers are paying well above European levels, dragging global prices higher. Separately, Congress is advancing legislation to break China's rare-earth grip before a November deadline, including four bills covering mine permits and a $2.5 billion reserve, per MSN/Bloomberg reporting. The EU-China trade feud over critical inputs is set for talks in Beijing on October 8–9.
sections.whyItMatters: A defense procurement deadline in Washington is now setting the global price of magnet metals. The West is paying a visible premium to build non-Chinese supply before the rules bite — and Beijing still controls the refining step that matters.

sections.heading: China Holds Back Fuel Exports, Squeezing Asia's Diesel
sections.body:
China has suspended oil product exports for October without official announcement, a move first reported by Reuters on October 1, leaving major refiners without the green light to export diesel, gasoline and jet fuel outside Hong Kong and Macau during the Golden Week holiday through Oct 7. CNA reported the suspension could tighten Asian diesel supplies with knock-on effects further afield.

'In the wider context of global diesel shortages, China's diesel export suspension is a blow to the Atlantic Basin balances,' June Goh, a senior oil market analyst at Sparta Commodities, told CNA, arguing Beijing is signaling it is 'not confident that the crude flows from the Middle East are going to remain protected from further attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.' China manages product shipments monthly and had relaxed curbs in July after tightening them in March.

Separately, Reuters columnists noted India may be best placed to fill part of the China-sized hole in fuel exports, given its refining capacity.
sections.whyItMatters: China is prioritizing its own holiday-season supply over export revenue, and its state refiners read the Gulf risk as unresolved. Diesel is the tightest product globally, so a one-month Chinese pause lands exactly where markets have the least slack.

sections.heading: Hormuz Shipping Attacks Hit LNG Carriers as Traffic Recovers
sections.body:
Attacks on commercial shipping around Hormuz continued, with LNG carriers now in the crosshairs. Twelve seafarers were injured — 11 of them Indian — when the Panama-flagged Aframax tanker On Peace was struck by a projectile in the strait, India's Ministry of External Affairs said, per gCaptain. Crew were evacuated with Omani help to Khasab. The vessel appears on a blacklist maintained by Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority. UKMTO issued four attack warnings and an advisory on Monday covering incidents dating to October 3.

A Greek-flagged LNG carrier, the Maran Gas Mystras, operated by Maran Gas Maritime, was struck near the waterline while leaving the strait and remained operational, the Cyprus Mail reported. It followed the October 4 strike on the Dynacom-managed tanker Lipsi, delivered just six weeks earlier. The IMO's register lists 93 confirmed incidents in the region.

Meanwhile Kpler data cited by International Finance shows Middle East crude exports back at pre-war levels — at least 16.5 mbd left the region between Sept 1 and 28, matching the pre-war average excluding Iran. But the route changed: only 40% crossed Hormuz, with more than 70% of crossing crude conducting offshore ship-to-ship transfers.
sections.whyItMatters: Volumes have recovered; the route has not. LNG is the new pressure point — Qatar's production has no alternative maritime exit, and September saw the most LNG shipments through the strait since the war began. Casualties among crews raise the odds of insurers and flag states tightening rules.

bottomLine: Two different price signals dominated the day. In oil, Saudi Arabia cut its Asian selling price to a six-year low to keep absorbing record freight costs, while the EIA raised its Brent forecast to about $98 for 2026 and about $105 for Q4 — producers and the US government both now treating the Gulf disruption as a lasting cost, not a spike. In power, Google's $4.3 billion, 890-MW nuclear deal with Constellation shows AI demand is becoming the West's most reliable financier of baseload capacity. Around both, the same unresolved questions persist: China is hoarding fuel, the EU is preparing its biggest Russia package yet while Russian diesel quietly flows in from South Korea, and heavy rare earth prices are spiking as the Pentagon's January 2027 sourcing ban approaches. The theme running through all of it is logistics and inputs — freight, refining, magnets — where the real bottlenecks now sit.
sources: Tekedia (Reuters data), Reuters, Utility Dive, Constellation Energy, 247wallst, EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook (via AJOT), UNN (Reuters), Army Recognition, The Guardian (via Irish Examiner), Fastmarkets, MSN/Bloomberg, CNA, gCaptain, Cyprus Mail, Kpler (via International Finance)
